## Victory, relative scoring and the random ending

The winner is the power that grew most relative to where it started, and nobody knows which turn will be the last. Both choices protect the core hypothesis: relative scoring keeps weak powers in contention, and an unknown end keeps reputation valuable until the final turn.

**Relative score.** Each power's strength, the wealth of its realm ("The wealth of a realm" below), is measured against its own starting strength. A Cyprus that doubles beats an Egypt that merely holds its ground. Strong powers face a higher bar, so they must expand, and everyone else has a reason to stop them.

**The wealth of a realm** (decided 21 October 2026). A power's strength is all the wealth in its land, counted as held and reckoned in gold. The land itself is valued at a multiple of what it produces (10 × its yield today; item 11+ settles how), counting the whole harvest and the mines' output at reference prices rather than the share the king takes, so a heavier tax adds nothing to the land's worth; that worth already shows the land's people, what has been built on it and what war has ravaged. A good's reference price is its base price, the price it fetches at its normal stock ("Prices"), set from the history pass and fixed within a game, so the score has one value per good and a famine or a cornered market moves no score. To the land add all the gold in the realm, in the treasury and in the people's purses of the provinces it holds, and the goods in its stores and in the markets of those provinces, at reference prices: grain in a market is as much the land's as grain in a store, so selling at home moves no score, and food costs score only when it is eaten. The realm's own gold and goods count wherever they are, in a caravan abroad or an army's baggage, until they change hands, and so does what its own men carry, soldiers', porters' and crews' savings and pay, since it goes home to the purse it came from; loot carried by loose men counts for no realm, like a character's gold, until it is spent or seized, so banditry shows as a loss at once and policing pays. Some things count only through what they do: units and walls are bought to win and keep wealth, and show in what they win and keep; buildings show in what they add to the yield, never in what they cost. What is owed counts neither way ("Debts are facts; repayment is a choice"). And characters' gold counts for no realm, even a hoard kept in the realm's own temple, since it belongs to a stranger who can leave with it; it counts in the characters' ranking instead, until a lord seizes it.

So every movement of wealth scores itself, with no rule of its own. Gold that stays in the land moves no score: the pay of soldiers and workers at home flows from the treasury into the people's purse, and the king's sales at his own markets draw it back, so a hoard in the treasury is worth exactly what the same gold is worth in his people's hands, and nothing rewards sitting on it. Wealth that crosses a border carries score with it: tribute, gifts, ransoms, tolls, loot, the price of goods bought and sold abroad, and the purses migrants carry ("Money moves with people") leave one realm and join another. It is moved, not made, so no two powers can conjure score by passing gold back and forth. Gold paid to a character, as a fee or a bribe, leaves every realm, and gold a character spends at a market joins the land he spends it in, so travellers and merchants enrich the lands they pass through, and part of every fee comes back where the man lives. Wealth enters the world only from the land, its harvests and its mines, and from the edge markets that trade with the world beyond the map ("Edge markets"), and it leaves only by use and ruin: food eaten, stores spoiled, fields burnt, ships sunk. A king who keeps his grain in store while his towns go hungry saves its price and loses more in people, at the land's multiple, and in the same season, since hunger answers in the season it bites (item 10+a). So a king spends abroad only when it buys more than it costs, as "Gold is a lifeline" already asks, and at home whenever it grows or guards the yield. What the score pays for in the moment, reputation answers: seizing a character's hoard or leaving a fee unpaid adds to the realm today and costs it a name for the rest of a game whose end nobody knows, and item 18 looks for such grabs by name. Egypt's mines still fill its treasury season by season, but par counts what a power that started where it did usually achieves ("One scoreboard for every power"), so Nubia's gold lifts Egypt only as far as it would anyway, and Egypt wins by what it does with it.

**Random ending** (revised 20 October 2026; drawn once, decided 21 October 2026). Any season may be the last, from the first. The chance starts very small and grows every season, so that the median game ends in 1332 BCE, the conventional date of the Amarna archive's end, about fourteen years or 44 seasons after the start in 1346 BCE. A game that may end at any time removes the safe final season for betrayal, and a chance that starts tiny keeps that uncertainty from the first season without cutting most games short. The engine draws the last season once, in secret, at the start, from that same rising chance and its own seeded stream, and the game ends at that season or at the cap, whichever comes first. It is the same game as drawing at the close of each season, with the same odds and the same replays, but no change elsewhere in the code can shift the end, and the balance pass can read the spread of game lengths straight from the seeds. The drawn season is a secret nothing shown may read: not the omens, which follow the public chance only ("Omens of the end"), not any seat's or character's request, not the look-ahead, and not a fallen player's god view. If the omens read it they would become a countdown, and the safe final season would be back.

- **First guess, for the builder:** a chance per season that grows in proportion to the season number: about 0.07% in the first season, 1% by season 15, 2% by season 30 and 3% by season 44. About one game in fourteen then ends before season 15, a quarter by season 30, half by season 44 and seven in ten by season 60. The hard cap is drawn in secret from 80 to 100 seasons (about 1320 to 1313 BCE), as a season rather than a year, so it can fall in any season; about one game in seventeen outlasts the rising chance to season 90, and about half of those meet the cap before it, so only about one in thirty plays season 90.
- **What kings are told:** the rule in words, not its numbers or the season: any season may be the last; early on it is very unlikely, and it grows likelier with every year. The hard cap is one of the numbers and stays secret too, so no seat can see a last season coming. When a table moves the median, the words follow it, in a few bands with no numbers (first guesses: an age likely to be short, of the usual length, or long). Every seat reads the same words, and a script king turns them into its belief of the curve, taking the band's own median rather than the table's number, so no seat knows more than the words say (decided 27 October 2026, answering item 6a's review). Characters are told the same rule from item 11a, since lending is the first thing they decide that depends on it, and see the omens from item 16 ("Omens of the end" below).
- **Tuning:** the exact curve is set in build order item 18, against how long wars now take (item 5 found a capital falling a median 9 to 10 seasons after the first entry). The cap and the median are settings (decided 21 October 2026): a table sets a range for the cap, or no cap, and can move the median earlier or later. The engine draws the real cap from that range in secret at the start, with the last season, so whoever sets up the game does not know the last season either; a range of a single season is a known cap, for a table that wants one. The defaults, a cap drawn from 80 to 100 seasons and a median about 1332 BCE, are only a starting point; item 18 evaluates them against how the game actually plays, weighing what longer games cost in usage against how exciting they stay, and sets the defaults from that. Whatever the table sets, no seat's request ever states the cap's number, and with no cap the omens simply follow the chance.
- **An open age.** A table may play with no end: no drawn last season and no cap, set at the start, or chosen when the age ends, to play on after the winner is recorded. Nothing else changes. The rulebook tells every seat the age has no end; scripts and models keep chasing growth against their start, which still means something with no end, and only the omens fall silent, with no end to foreshadow. A game with no end makes model calls with no end, so a table that opens the age with any model-played seat sets its spending limit by hand, never left at the default, before the game starts or plays on, and the game pauses when it is reached (decided 27 October 2026, answering item 6a's review); from item 6c it also sets what a season may cost ("Minds follow what is at stake").

**Omens of the end (decided 21 October 2026).** The rising chance is shown, not stated. Each season every court's diviners read the signs in the voice of the age (Babylonian liver readers, Hittite augurs, Egypt's lector priests, Alashiya's eagle diviners, and the royal council's Diviner where the council is on), and the signs darken as the chance grows. They show the public chance only, never the drawn season ("Random ending"), so they darken by the curve alone, nobody can foresee the date from them, and they stay seeded and deterministic. Characters are told the rule and see the omens too, since they lend, borrow and plan by them; a lender asking more as the signs darken is his own reading, and no rule sets rates. The end itself is the age turning, the archive closing for every court, not anything that befalls Egypt in the game, since Egypt may have fallen by then. The historical tie stays in the background: the median ending falls about when the real court left Akhetaten and its archive of letters was left behind. Presentation only: no rule checks an omen. Built with the royal council (build order item 16), for every seat and character whether or not the council is on.

How the omens darken:

- **In tiers, never in numbers.** The signs move through a few tiers as the chance grows, from quiet to troubled to grave.
- **Borrowed time past the median.** Once a game passes a point drawn in secret near the median ending, so that the change of tone does not reveal the median, which kings are not told, the diviners begin to say that the age has outlived its measure: the signs have long pointed to an end that has not come. The tone changes, not only the strength.
- **The darkest tier comes well before the cap, and stays.** If the wording kept worsening to the last season, a careful player could read the secret cap from it, so the darkest tier is reached at the bottom of the cap's range (season 80 by default), not at some distance before the drawn cap, so it reveals nothing beyond the range itself, and then held, and the end comes as suddenly at the cap as at any season.

Each court reads the signs in its own diviners' voice, after how they spoke in this period and the ones next to it:

- **Babylonia, Assyria and Mitanni: the liver.** Their diviners read the sheep's liver and wrote what they saw as an omen: if this mark is there, then this will happen to the king, the army or the land. Some omens named a fallen king as the precedent, such as the destruction omen of Ibbi-Sin, the last king of Ur, so the darkest tier can be a liver that bears such a mark.
- **Hatti and Arzawa: oracles that answer yes or no.** Hittite diviners asked one question at a time, by the liver, by the flight of birds, or by the lots of the Old Woman, and each answer came back favourable or unfavourable; they chained questions to find which god was angry and why. The darkest tier is every question answered unfavourable. Mursili II's prayers against the plague, a generation later, show how a Hittite court spoke when the gods' anger would not lift.
- **Egypt: the gods turning away.** Tutankhamun's Restoration Stela, set up a few years after the archive's end, describes a land in distress whose gods "were turning away from this land": an army sent north had no success, and "if one prayed to a god to ask a thing of him, he wouldn't come." Egypt's darkest tier speaks in that voice.
- **Alashiya: the eagle diviner.** Cyprus's king asked Pharaoh for "a specialist in eagle-omens", and blamed a short shipment of copper on "the hand of Nergal", the plague god, in his land (EA 35). Its omens come from birds and from that hand.

The lines are written fresh in these voices and quote the sources where a line fits. Sources: the [Restoration Stela](https://sites.cs.st-andrews.ac.uk/egyptian/texts/corpus/pdf/RestorationTutankhamun.pdf); [Hittite divination](https://wres-hatti.adwudlit.uni-mainz.de/HPM/hpm-en.php?p=divin-en); [liver omens, Ibbi-Sin's among them](https://cojs.org/?p=4887); [EA 35](https://ancientegyptonline.co.uk/ea35/). The historical sources pass (build order item 6+) gathers more for each court.

**When one power is left (decided 21 October 2026).** The game also ends when only one power is left standing, since nothing is left to measure it against. A vassal is still a power of its own, so holding vassals is not the same as having taken them. Built with the scoreboard in build order item 11+.

**Why not a fixed end.** If everyone knows turn 20 is last, a promise is worthless in the final rounds and every game ends in mass betrayal. Game theory calls this losing the shadow of the future.

**Shared victory (off).** One power wins: the one with the highest growth. Shared victory is kept only as an optional house rule. As built, it could only add the leader's ally to the winners, paid for a flag on a sealed tablet rather than a kept oath, and any alliance made the condition easier. Without it, alliances hold or break only on what each king expects of the other. The rulebook and order schema mention it only when the house rule is on, so model kings never read it otherwise.

**Two kinds of threat.** Under relative scoring, kings face two different dangers. Absolute strength nearby is a security threat: a large neighbor can attack you. Relative growth is a victory threat: a small kingdom doubling in size can win. The two pull apart, and that tension is deliberate: in the setting no Great King fears a growing Cyprus, but under the scoring he should. Script kings weigh both, with the balance varying by temperament (a cautious king watches the neighbor, an ambitious one watches whoever grows fastest); model kings work it out from the rulebook.

**Scoring.** Strength is already economic value: 10 × the yield of land held, plus gold, with units counting nothing; from build order item 9+a it becomes the wealth of the realm, the people's purses and the goods in stores and markets included ("The wealth of a realm"). Back pay owed and debts on sealed debt tablets do not count against it: the score counts what a kingdom holds, and unpaid fees and debts are answered by the world ("Jobs, not wages"; "Debts are facts; repayment is a choice"; decided 21 October 2026). The built score still subtracts back pay until build order item 11a changes it. Until build order item 11+, buying a city is score-neutral at the moment of purchase, since its price is what it adds to strength: 10 × yield, and from item 9+a its purse, stores and market as well. The price leaves the world, paid to the city's notables, whom the game does not model ("Where gold comes from and where it goes"); paid into the city's own purse, it would come back to the buyer and make buying pure gain. From item 11+ there is no purchase, and the comparison changes to par for each starting position ("One scoreboard for every power" below). Two things remain:

- **Neutrality is accidental.** It rests on two separate settings that happen to match: one shared score function already serves the engine and the bots, but the city price, until item 11+ removes buying, is still a setting of its own rather than derived from the score weight. Whatever the score becomes, the kings' victory-threat assessment must use the same function, applied to their estimates of rivals, so bots pursue exactly what the game rewards.
- **Normalization waits for data.** A raw ratio swings harder for small powers, but in script games the strong powers still win most. Decided 20 October 2026: par against expected results for each starting position ("One scoreboard for every power" below), designed in item 11+ and tuned in item 18 from script games.

**One scoreboard for every power** (decided 20 October 2026). Great Kings and city-states are the same kind of player: the same orders, envoys and characters, the same goal, judged on one scoreboard. A king who falls to a single city is then simply a small power, and nothing makes it pay to stay small or to avoid becoming great.

- **What counts is physics, measurable and slow to turn:** the wealth of the realm, counted as held, debts left out ("The wealth of a realm"). Relations never count, since words can change in a season, and a vassal counts only through the tribute he actually pays, which leaves his realm and joins his overlord's as it arrives ("What a breach means, and to whom" under Written agreements).
- **What changes is the comparison.** A power is measured against par for its starting position: what a power that started where it did usually achieves, from script games. A one-city power and an empire then have a comparable chance to win, and different powers emerge as winners.
- **A vassal is on the same scoreboard as its overlord,** so a vassal growing strong is a rival, and an overlord has reason to keep his vassals useful but not too strong.
- **To design in build order item 11+ and tune in item 18:** how par is computed, and how the land weighs against gold and goods: at a fixed multiple of what it produces, or perhaps as the gold it can still produce in the seasons a game is likely to have left, though that makes land cheaper against gold as the omens darken.

**Later variant** (set aside on 21 October 2026 by "Each court plays differently, with no mission tree"). Hidden individual objectives, such as holding a region or reaching a treasury, create goals that are not fully opposed and room for deals.
